**Also sprach Zarathustra (Thus Spoke Zarathustra)**
Strauss's 1896 tone poem, subtitled "freely after Nietzsche" and based on Friedrich Nietzsche's philosophical novel. It is by far his most common giveaway, made famous by its use at the opening of Stanley Kubrick's film 2001: A Space Odyssey, which also used Johann Strauss II's Blue Danube (a different, unrelated composer). Its sections include "Of Science and Learning," "The Grave-Song," and "The Song of the Night Wanderer," which ends unresolved with the keys B major (humanity) and C major (nature or the universe) set against each other.

**"Sunrise" and the C–G–C "nature" motif**
The opening of Zarathustra: over a low organ and contrabassoon pedal, trumpets play the rising notes C–G–C, called the "nature" or "world riddle" motif, followed by a full orchestral chord and pounding timpani. It represents the sun rising.

**Salome**
Strauss's 1905 one-act opera based on Oscar Wilde's play, considered shocking and blasphemous at its premiere. Salome, stepdaughter of King Herod, demands the head of the prophet Jochanaan (John the Baptist). Before this, Herod slips in the blood of the guard captain Narraboth, who has killed himself, and imagines he hears the beating of wings.

**Dance of the Seven Veils and the kiss of the severed head**
In Salome, the title character performs the seductive Dance of the Seven Veils for Herod in return for Jochanaan's head. In the final scene she kisses the severed head while the orchestra plays a famously dissonant chord, sometimes called "the most sickening chord in all opera." Horrified, Herod orders his soldiers to crush her to death under their shields.

**Der Rosenkavalier (The Knight of the Rose)**
Strauss's 1911 comic opera with a libretto by Hugo von Hofmannsthal, set in 18th-century Vienna. The young Count Octavian, a trouser role sung by a mezzo-soprano, is sent to present a ceremonial silver rose to Sophie von Faninal for her engagement, but the two fall in love at first sight.

**Baron Ochs and "Mariandel"**
The crude, boorish Baron Ochs is Sophie's intended husband in Der Rosenkavalier. Octavian disguises himself as a chambermaid named "Mariandel," whom Ochs tries to seduce, and with the help of the Italian intriguers Valzacchi and Annina sets a trap that humiliates Ochs and ruins his marriage plans. The opera ends with the young Black page Mohammed running onstage to fetch a dropped handkerchief.

**The Marschallin and the trio "Hab mir's gelobt"**
The Marschallin, an aging princess and Octavian's older lover, gracefully gives him up to Sophie and resolves to love even "his love for another." Her final-act trio "Hab mir's gelobt" is sung by three female voices because Octavian is a trouser role, and it is followed by the Octavian–Sophie duet "Ist ein Traum." Georg Solti conducted the trio at Strauss's funeral. In an earlier monologue she admits that she sometimes stops all the clocks at night.

**Elektra**
Strauss's 1909 opera, his first with librettist Hofmannsthal, based on Sophocles' tragedy about Agamemnon's daughter seeking revenge for her father's murder. In her monologue "Allein! Weh, ganz allein," Elektra sings her father's name to the opening Agamemnon motif. The "Elektra chord," E major and C-sharp (D-flat) major triads played at the same time, expresses her violent emotions.

**Till Eulenspiegel's Merry Pranks**
An 1895 tone poem about the German folk trickster Till Eulenspiegel. A rollicking French horn theme and a shrill D clarinet represent Till. At the end he is tried and led to the gallows, and his death is shown by a squawking high clarinet.

**Ein Heldenleben (A Hero's Life)**
A semi-autobiographical 1898 tone poem that opens with rising E-flat major triads representing the hero. Its sections include "The Hero's Adversaries" (critics, depicted by grumbling woodwinds and tubas playing a motif in parallel fifths), "The Hero's Companion" (a violin solo portraying his wife), "The Hero's Battlefield," and "The Hero's Works of Peace," which quotes Strauss's own earlier works.

**An Alpine Symphony**
A 1915 tone poem in 22 continuous sections that is called a symphony even though it is not one in the traditional sense. It portrays a day climbing a mountain, inspired by a climb Strauss made as a boy, with sections like "Entry into the Forest," "Wandering by the Brook," "On the Summit," "Thunderstorm," and "Descent." It uses a wind machine, a thunder machine, offstage brass for a hunting party, and a heckelphone, whose low written notes led to the invention of the lupophon.

**Four Last Songs**
Strauss's final major work, for soprano and orchestra, written in 1948 when he was in his 80s and published after his death by his friend Ernst Roth. Three songs set poems by Hermann Hesse ("Spring," "September," and "When Falling Asleep"). The fourth, "Im Abendrot" ("At Sunset"), sets Joseph von Eichendorff and depicts an old couple at sunset, with two trilling flutes as larks, and ends "Is this perhaps death?" Strauss wanted Kirsten Flagstad to give the premiere.

**Metamorphosen**
A 1945 elegy for 23 solo strings, written near the end of World War II as German cities and opera houses were being destroyed. Near the end, the cellos and basses quote the funeral march from Beethoven's Eroica Symphony, and Strauss wrote "IN MEMORIAM!" in the score at that point.

**Symphonia Domestica (Domestic Symphony)**
An autobiographical 1903 tone poem depicting a day in Strauss's household with his wife and baby son, including bathing the baby. A glockenspiel strikes seven to show the hour. In a love scene, an oboe solo is interrupted by the sound of the baby crying.

**Death and Transfiguration (Tod und Verklärung)**
An 1889 tone poem portraying the last moments of a dying artist, his memories, and his soul's transfiguration after death. It is often grouped with his other early tone poems Don Juan and Don Quixote, the latter featuring a large solo cello as the knight and bleating sheep imitated by flutter-tongued brass.
